title: Eurozone Inflation Jumps to 3.8% in September, a Three-Year High, on Energy Costs
excerpt: Energy prices surged 18.8% on the year as oil topped $105 a barrel, beating economists' 3.6% forecast and piling pressure on the ECB ahead of its October 29 meeting.
body:
• Eurozone inflation rose to 3.8% year-on-year in September, up from 3.2% in August — the fastest price growth since September 2023, and above the 3.6% economists expected.
  • Energy prices did the damage: up 18.8% on the year, near the sharpest rise since 2022, as Brent crude topped $105 a barrel and natural gas climbed ahead of winter.
  • Core inflation edged up to 2.5% and services to 3.2%, signs the shock may be seeping into the wider economy — the outcome the ECB fears most.
  • ECB President Christine Lagarde told EU lawmakers the shock was "too large to look through," with the deposit rate at 2.5% and the next policy meeting set for October 29.

Inflation in the eurozone jumped to its highest level in three years last month, driven by a sharp acceleration in energy prices, according to flash estimates released Friday by Eurostat, the European Union's statistics office. Consumer prices were 3.8% higher in September than the same month a year earlier, up from an annual rate of 3.2% in August — the fastest rise since September 2023 and well above the European Central Bank's 2% target.

The reading beat expectations: economists polled by The Wall Street Journal had forecast 3.6%, a survey taken before higher-than-expected prints this week from member states including France and Italy. Energy prices were 18.8% higher than a year ago, nearing the steepest annual rise since 2022, when Russia halted natural gas supplies to pressure Europe over its support for Ukraine.

"While the shock is too large to look through, we view a measured response as appropriate to keep inflation in check."

— Christine Lagarde, President, European Central Bank

Energy leads, but the shock is spreading

Escalating military action in the Middle East sent Brent crude oil above $105 a barrel at points in September, and natural gas prices have risen as Europe stocks up for winter. That flowed directly into the inflation basket: fuel and power did most of the damage, with energy inflation accelerating from 14.3% in August to 18.8% in September.

The more worrying detail for Frankfurt is what is happening beyond the petrol pump. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, edged up to 2.5% from 2.4% in August. Services inflation climbed to 3.2% from 3.0%, while food, alcohol and tobacco inflation accelerated to 1.4%. Euro 95 petrol hit an all-time high, according to analysis by ING economist Bert Colijn, and wage-growth indicators have risen for five consecutive months — the classic early signals of second-round effects.

An energy shock is unpleasant. An energy shock embedded in wages, services and business costs is considerably more troublesome, as consumers and companies begin to assume prices will keep rising and inflation acquires a momentum of its own.

The ECB's ugly choice

The central bank faces the oldest monetary-policy dilemma: raise interest rates and risk damaging growth, or hold back and risk letting inflation entrench. The ECB in September raised its key interest rate for the second time this year, to 2.5%, saying it could not ignore the jump in energy prices. Inflation has been above its 2% target since March.

Yet there is a complication: government bond yields have jumped in recent weeks, tightening financial conditions without any further action from Frankfurt. That may make the bank wary of lifting rates again. Markets are not expecting an October increase, with the next move not fully priced in until January — though this print, landing ahead of the ECB's October 29 meeting, will test that calm.

Broad and getting broader

The acceleration is not confined to one corner of the bloc. Among the euro area's largest economies, inflation accelerated in Germany to 3.3% from 2.9%, France to 3.4% from 2.6%, Italy to 4.1% from 3.2%, and the Netherlands to 3.0% from 2.8%. Spain led the pack at 5.0%, up from 4.6%.

For investors, the release lands alongside a weak US jobs report that sent bonds rallying — a cross-current of slowing American growth and re-accelerating European inflation that leaves global rate expectations unusually muddled heading into the fourth quarter. A hawkish ECB adds to global yield pressure and keeps the euro firm against currencies like the rupee, a consideration for Indian investors with the RBI's own policy decision due on October 7.

What to watch

Three questions now matter. First, whether the energy shock stays contained or feeds further into core prices and services over the coming months — the core reading at the next print will be scrutinised as closely as the headline. Second, how the Middle East conflict and winter gas demand shape energy prices through the fourth quarter. Third, what the ECB actually does on October 29: another hike would squeeze an already fragile growth picture, but standing still risks repeating the mistake of underestimating an energy-driven surge.
